Twenty Fifth Indian Antarctic Expedition 2006-2007
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 23, pp 223-234
Exploration of Microbial Diversity from Antarctica 
with Special Emphasis on Biotechnological Potential
Shailendra Sonawane, Girish Mahajan, Saji George,
P. Giridharan, Asha Almeida and P. D. Mishra
Piramal Life Sciences Limited, Nirlon Complex,
Goregaon, Mumbai 400063, India
ABSTRACT
During the XXV expedition 60 soil samples were collected from different 
localities of Schirmacher Oasis, Antarctica. It includes mosses, lichen and sediment 
samples. The soil samples were processed to isolate microbes. These microbes 
were further fermented in different media and metabolite extract library was 
prepared. The metabolite extracts were evaluated for their biological activity in 
therapeutic areas such as anti-infective, anticancer and anti-inflammation. The 
promising extracts were subjected for chemical investigation to isolate bioactive 
principles.
INTRODUCTION
Actinomycetes, myxobacteria and certain other eubacteria of the genus 
bacillus have always been a major source of bioactive compounds. 
Especially actinomycetes are always in the frontline as a source of novel 
bioactive molecules. The redundancy level in the compounds isolated from 
the microbesVas been increasing over the period. To reduce this one of the 
smart way is to look for microbes from unexplored natural resources. 
Microbes with tailored metabolism in these extreme geographic locations 
do display a different secondary metabolism, which enhances the prospect 
of yielding novel compounds with altered mechanism of actions in living 
cells.
During the past 2-3 decades, interest in glacier microflora increased 
due to the investigation of novel bioactive compounds, especially antibiotics 
and enzymes activate in low temperatures. Due to severe environmental 
conditions (low temperature, low humidity, high radiation etc). Antarctica 
is a representation of a unique resource of microbes with distorted 
metabolism. The continent of Antarctica is a major cold habitat, covering

about 14 million square kilometers of which all but 2% is covered by ice 
and snow. Nonetheless, it is far from uniform and has environmental niches, 
including different soil types, sediments, rocks and melt waters, as well as 
snow and ice, that vary in the constancy of their thermal regime, nutrient 
status, water activity and salinity. These factors are important in nourishing 
certain selected micro flora in those areas. It is also reflected in the wide 
diversity of cold adapted micro-organisms that include bacteria, archaea, 
yeast, fungi and micro algae. While exploring the continental glacial samples 
and those of shelves and icebergs, a lot of sporulating and non-sporulating 
bacteria, some yeasts species, fungi and Actinomycetes were found. New 
microbial species are being reported more frequently from Antarctic region. 
This is illustrated by reports of new actinomyces species like Friedmanella 
Antarctica,Friedmanella lacustris,Nocardiopsis aurantiacus, and 
Modestobacterium multiseptatum.
In the present study we are presenting the work done at Piramal Life 
Science limited for the resource samples collected from Antarctic region 
in XXV expedition in collaboration with National Center for Antarctic 
and Ocean Research. Microbes isolated from different habitat from 
Antarctica were cultured in the laboratory conditions. Microbial studies 
were carried out with the purified isolates. These microbial isolates were 
explored for their therapeutic potentials.
Sample Collection
Detailed survey of various geographical regions was conducted at 
Schirmacher Oasis, Antarctica with the purpose of tapping novel microbial 
biodiversity on the basis of literature search (Annexure I). During the 
expedition we collected 60 different soil samples from 30 different identified 
locations. All these identified soil samples were collected in aseptic 
conditions and transferred to sterile plastic bags which later were stored at 
-20°C until it reached the laboratory for further processing.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Soil Sample Maintenance
The soil samples collected from Antarctic regions were maintained 
at -20°C to avoid any deterioration or decay of the samples.
Isolation of Actinomycetes and other Eubacteria

maintained on ice bath (0-2°C) for slow thawing. All the samples were
